item.title: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose
item.description:
Background: Layperson-administered naloxone is increasingly common before emergency medical services (EMS) arrival. However, EMS care following naloxone administered by laypeople rather than trained responders remains poorly characterized.

Methods: This cross-sectional study used the 2023 National EMS Information System dataset and included 9-1-1 activations for individuals aged ≥ 16 years with an EMS impression of opioid overdose and documented naloxone administration before EMS arrival. Exposures were layperson-administered naloxone (LAN) or trained responder-administered naloxone (TRAN; e.g., police, firefighter). The primary outcome was subsequent EMS naloxone administration. Secondary outcomes included total number of EMS naloxone administrations, advanced airway intervention, cardiac arrest, and EMS transport. We used descriptive statistics, t-tests, and multivariable logistic regression estimating adjusted odds ratios (aOR).

Results: Among 26,087 EMS activations, 8016 (30.7%) received LAN and 18,071 (69.3%) TRAN. Any subsequent EMS naloxone administration was less frequent following LAN (24.4% vs. 34.8%; P < .001); when EMS did administer additional naloxone, the mean number of administrations was slightly higher following LAN (mean difference 0.05, 95%CI 0.02-0.09; P = .001). Advanced airway attempts (1.6% vs. 1.4%, P = .160) and cardiac arrest (6.6% vs. 6.0%, P = .080) were uncommon. EMS transport occurred less often after LAN (79.4% vs. 84.4%, P < .001). In adjusted analyses, LAN was associated with lower odds of subsequent EMS naloxone administration (aOR 0.73; 95%CI 0.68-0.78) and EMS transport (aOR 0.78; 95%CI 0.73-0.84).

Conclusions: Layperson-administered naloxone was associated with less frequent EMS naloxone administration and lower rates of EMS transport. These findings support layperson overdose response while highlighting the need to better understand post-overdose care trajectories.

Ulintz AJ, Gage CB, Kamholz JC, Riel KM, van den Bergh SL, Lyons MS

item.title: Association between telehealth utilization and buprenorphine treatment retention among rural Veterans with opioid use disorder
item.description:
Introduction: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a major public health challenge that disproportionately impacts Veterans, 34% of whom live rurally. Buprenorphine medication treatment for OUD (B-MOUD) is a first-line treatment and telehealth expansion has improved its access. This study aimed to determine whether the extent of telehealth use is associated with differences in B-MOUD retention among rural Veterans with OUD.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of rural Veterans who initiated B-MOUD within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) from 2021 to 2024. Telehealth utilization within a B-MOUD episode of care (EoC) was categorized based on the proportion of encounters delivered via telehealth (TH): no TH (0%), minority TH (>0%&≤50%), and majority TH (>50%). Retention was measured as the number of days from EoC start to treatment discontinuation (final day covered before >30-day gap). Restricted mean retention time (RMRT), defined as the mean time retained in treatment up to 90- and 180-days, was estimated using adjusted Kaplan-Meier curves.

Results: There were 10,875 B-MOUD EoC among 7012 Veterans. At 90 days, RMRT was 73.0(95% CI 72.0-73.3) days for no TH, 82.6(81.9-83.0) for minority TH, and 82.6(82.0-82.9) for majority TH groups. At 180 days, RMRT was 115.1(112.7-116.2), 148.3(146.4-149.4), and 143.2(141.4-144.2) days, respectively. Median number of days to discontinuation was longest for minority (338[314-366]), followed by majority (247[233-269]) and no TH (119[113-126]) groups.

Conclusion: Telehealth utilization was associated with greater B-MOUD retention compared to no telehealth utilization among rural Veterans, with the highest retention observed when telehealth comprised ≤ 50% of visits, supporting the value of flexible, multimodal care delivery.

Carriera S, Baylis JD, Stofko A, Huebler S, Kertesz SG, Wyse JJ

item.title: Associations between patient-reported alcohol screening scores, alcohol use disorder symptoms, and suicidality in a large primary care sample
item.description:
Background: Most people who attempt or die by suicide were recently seen in primary care, and alcohol use increases suicide risk. This study examined associations between alcohol consumption and alcohol use disorder (AUD) severity with multiple suicidality measures among primary care patients with screening-identified depression.

Methods: We analyzed electronic health record and insurance claims data from Kaiser Permanente Washington (KPWA) primary care patients who completed routine depression and alcohol screenings and screened positive for depression on a brief screen. Generalized estimating equation models evaluated associations between alcohol-related assessments (Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test-Consumption [AUDIT-C]; AUD severity via Alcohol Symptom Checklist), and suicidality measures (thoughts of self-harm or death, suicidal ideation/intention/planning, and suicide-related acute care utilization over 1 year).

Results: Thoughts of self-harm or death were associated with high-risk (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR]=1.13, 95% confidence interval: [1.08-1.19]) and very high-risk alcohol use (aPR=1.31 [1.23-1.39]), as well as moderate AUD (aPR=1.24 [1.08-1.41]) and severe AUD (aPR=1.45 [1.30-1.61]). Suicidal ideation/planning/intent were higher across moderate to very high-risk AUDIT-C categories and in patients reporting symptoms consistent with severe AUD. Suicide-related acute care utilization was associated higher across non-drinking, high-risk, and very high-risk AUDIT-C categories and in patients reporting symptoms consistent with severe AUD.

Conclusion: Among primary care patients who screened positive for depression, the AUDIT-C and Alcohol Symptom Checklist can provide clinically useful information for suicide risk assessment to primary care clinicians. It may be beneficial to jointly implement depression and alcohol screening to help integrate alcohol-focused and suicide prevention efforts in primary care.

Chang Y, Matson TE, Frost MC, Lee ML, Oliver M, Jack HE

item.title: Day-level mediators of change in a brief motivational intervention for alcohol use and liver health
item.description:
Background: Day-level motivation to limit drinking is theorized to be a proximal mechanism of change in motivational interviewing (MI), but day-level evidence remains limited. This study examined whether brief MI with personalized biobehavioral feedback was associated with changes in daily drinking among adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD), including a subgroup with co-occurring alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), and whether day-level importance and confidence to limit drinking served as within-person mediators.

Methods: Participants (N = 33; M age = 46.0 [12.55]; 799 day-level observations) completed morning surveys for 28 days, including up to 10 pre-intervention days. Each morning, they reported the prior day's standard drinks and rated that day's importance and confidence to limit drinking on 0-10 scales. Multilevel interrupted time-series models included a pre-intervention slope, an intervention-day level shift, and a post-intervention slope, and tested day-level importance and confidence as mediators of daily drinking outcomes.

Results: Daily drinking declined during the pre-intervention period, with no significant intervention-day shifts or post-intervention trends. The intervention-day shift was associated with higher day-level importance of limiting drinking, and higher-than-usual importance and confidence on a given day were associated with fewer planned and actual drinks and lower odds of any and heavy drinking. The intervention-day shift was associated, indirectly, with lower daily drinking through higher same-day importance.

Conclusions: Intensive longitudinal data supported perceived importance of limiting drinking as a proximal mediator of change in brief AUD/ALD interventions, suggesting that frequent, day-level reinforcement of the personal salience of drinking reduction may be a key intervention target.

Aggarwal A, Monti PM, Magill M, Promrat K, Mellinger JL, Treloar Padovano H

item.title: Use of anabolic androgenic steroids in a Swedish forensic population: Associations with substance use and criminal convictions
item.description:
Background: The use of anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS) has been associated with adverse psychiatric effects and risk behavior, including increased aggressiveness. The aim of this study was to characterize AAS users in forensic settings and investigate criminal convictions, the use of other substances and sociodemographic factors.

Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional study used Swedish national register data. The study included 3548 men who tested positive for AAS at the National Board of Forensic Medicine between 2010 and 2022. The study population consisted of individuals undergoing forensic toxicological analysis following requests from the police. AAS-positive (AAS-pos) individuals were compared with 6595 men who tested negative for AAS (AAS-neg) and a matched control group of 17,744 men not tested for AAS.

Results: The prevalence of AAS was 35% and testosterone was the most frequently determined AAS. The AAS-pos group had a median of 2.0 rearrests during a two-year follow-up. Concomitant use of illicit and/or licit substances was observed in 50% of the AAS-pos individuals. Cannabis, followed by amphetamines, were the most commonly determined illicit substances across all groups. Compared with the other groups, AAS-pos individuals were more frequently sentenced to imprisonment (p < 0.05). Drug offences showed the largest difference between AAS-pos and AAS-neg individuals. A similar profile was observed for weapons offences.

Conclusion: AAS use in this forensic setting is linked to a pattern of risk behavior characterized by substance use and criminal involvement.

Lood Y, Jönsson AK, Ahlner F, Chermá MD
